name: Eugenic feminism
summary: Eugenic feminism, a term Caleb Saleeby coined in 1911, joins support for women's votes and legal equality with the aim of improving the inherited quality of the next generation through women's choice of fathers, through motherhood treated as the nation's chief work and through limits on unfit parenthood. It treats the sexes as biologically different and interdependent, opposes sex-antagonism, and wants men made legally responsible for supporting mothers and children. The Canadian suffragists the Eugenics Archive describes carried it into public health and sterilisation law.
scope: The branch of early feminism the Eugenics Archive describes: Saleeby's eugenic feminism as set out in Woman and Womanhood (1911), the Canadian suffragists it names (McClung, Murphy and the Famous Five: the vote, motherhood, Alberta's 1928 Sexual Sterilization Act, pre-marriage health certificates), and the birth-control and sex-education case the Archive lists among its positions (it names Sanger, whose text is not used because the defining sources name her only once). Gilman is left out: the defining sources do not name her as an eugenic feminist, and Saleeby disputes her economic independence and nursery proposals. Fiction (Herland) and later writers are not used.

missingStatements.rationale: Saleeby makes the father's legal duty to support mother and children the centre of his answer on the rights of mothers.

quotes.text: Assuredly the unmarried father must be held responsible; and no less certainly must we see to it that, with or without his help, the unmarried mother and her children are adequately provided for.

missingStatements.rationale: Saleeby treats women's choice of fathers by natural quality as the central eugenic duty of women.

quotes.text: No one can attach more than its due importance to woman's function of choosing the fathers of the future; rejecting the unworthy and selecting the worthy for this greatest of human duties.

quotes.text: But the point to be insisted upon is that it is far more worth her while to choose for natural quality than for any other considerations.

notes: Scope follows the Eugenics Archive entries (Women's suffrage and Feminism), which name Saleeby as coiner, McClung, Murphy and Sanger as eugenic feminists; Gilman is not named there and Saleeby disputes her, so she is out. Saleeby's text is the primary source; Sanger's Woman and the New Race was downloaded but not used because the defining sources name her only once. Saleeby's text answers about 30 statements; the Archive adds the sterilisation, education and birth-control record,. Themes searched in Saleeby's full text and the Archive: suffrage, divorce, marriage and monogamy, motherhood and endowment, alcohol, war, race, immigration, trade and fiscal policy, socialism and individualism, education and sex instruction, abortion and sterilisation, nature versus nurture. Emily Murphy's The Black Candle (1922, a drug-control book the Archive names) was downloaded to the local library but not used: it speaks for one member and says nothing on the other lines. Race, immigration, economy, government form, foreign policy beyond war and trade, religion and ecology are largely unaddressed in the sources, so many lines stay null.
